0.notes: D-dominant: SWRCB water rights licensing and OCWD basin management impose strong constraints. Multiple rights holders (OCWD + ~30 municipal agencies) introduce D-C fragmentation even at Phase 0.
0.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

1.notes: Multiple municipal agencies abstract independently; no coordinated reporting. Contrast with NEWater where single PUB actor operates all abstraction.
1.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

2.notes: Fragmented: each of ~30 agencies operates its own treatment plant. Published compliance data at state level but granular inter-agency comparison not easily available.
2.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

3.notes: Highly fragmented: each agency has its own storage infrastructure. No centralised reporting of aggregate storage at reservoir-level.
3.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

4.notes: High per-capita consumption versus compact urban benchmarks (75 vs 38 gallons/day). California conservation mandates attempt to reduce this.
4.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

5.notes: New actor enters: OC San. Separate billing structure (sewer service charge distinct from water charge); separate governing board. D-C discontinuity begins here.
5.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

6.notes: OC San operates. Reasonable transparency via NPDES permit compliance; but OC San's opaque inter-agency cost allocation reduces D-C coherence.
6.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

7.notes: Still OC San at this event. The HANDOFF to OCWD occurs at Event 10 (Phase 8 boundary) — the largest single D-C discontinuity in this chain. OC San and OCWD have separate governing boards, separate finances, and negotiate the secondary effluent supply agreement separately.
7.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

8.notes: FIRST MAJOR INSTITUTIONAL HANDOFF: OC San secondary effluent → OCWD GWRS. B9=true, B10=true. Two separate legal entities with separate governance and finances negotiate the secondary effluent supply agreement. This boundary crossing is the largest institutional cost driver. Treatment cost: ~USD 1.25/m³ (OCWD Annual Report FY2023-24 operational data). Energy: ~4.2 kWh/m³ (RO-dominated; OCWD 2023).
8.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

9.notes: California regulatory framework is complex due to multi-agency oversight (SWRCB, DDW, Regional Water Quality Control Boards). Each layer adds D constraint without proportional C integration.
9.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

10.notes: SECOND INSTITUTIONAL TRANSITION: OCWD injects into shared groundwater commons. Water passes from OCWD control into a basin accessed by ~30 independent agencies. The downstream distribution is NOT under OCWD's institutional control — contrast with NEWater where PUB operates its own dedicated distribution network.
10.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input

11.notes: STRUCTURAL THOLONIC GAP: Phase 11 child-N does NOT close back to Phase 0 through a single actor. Water enters a shared groundwater commons controlled by OCWD but pumped by ~30 independent municipal agencies. The tholonic recursion — Phase 11 child-N becoming Phase 0 parent-N — is BROKEN at this point. OCWD cannot ensure that the water it recycled is the same water that returns to Phase 1 via any specific agency. Compare NEWater: PUB blends into its own reservoirs and controls re-abstraction directly. This structural gap is predicted by the Tholonic model to produce lower N stability and higher system cost — confirmed by the USD 0.35/m3 institutional treatment cost premium.
11.scope_source: Not provided — requires separate data input
